_Why can individually tested components still leave an agent's task unfinished or its effects unaccounted for?_

An autonomous agent unites disparate systems disciplines (foundation models, memory hierarchies, isolated execution sandboxes, transactional event logs, and independent verifiers) into a single closed-loop control architecture. Each individual component can satisfy its local unit tests, yet the integrated system can still fail if the contracts connecting them are ungrounded or ambiguous. The core challenge of agentic systems engineering is designing the deterministic harness that bounds and verifies a stochastic proposer, a problem that larger models and more elaborate prompts do not remove. Across a trajectory horizon, carried working state, and delegated authority, reliable autonomy is achieved only when the runtime enforces invariant closure at every system boundary.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Trace an incident-remediation trajectory, identifying the owner and record of each consequential transition
- Translate a task contract into bounds and acceptance requirements proportionate to its horizon, state, and authority
- Diagnose state and evidence mismatches at subsystem boundaries using the authority and lifetime of each record
- Resolve an uncertain external action without confusing a lost response with permission to repeat its effect
- Select a system intervention using attributed failures, outcome evidence, and its full deployment cost
- Construct a safety case that connects scoped claims to arguments, evidence, assumptions, and residual uncertainty
- Distinguish assistance with specifications from authority to adopt them and accept the resulting task

:::
## Answers to the Three Questions {#sec-vol3-conclusion-questions}

Every mechanism in the book now carries a price in one unit, the cost per accepted task of each lighthouse (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-synthesis). The three architectural questions posed in the introduction, each answered in part by every later chapter, therefore admit concise engineering answers, and each answer is a design claim that one live operational workload can test.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The three foundational architectural questions governing agentic design are established in @sec-vol3-intro-questions.
:::

The first question asked when an adaptive, model-directed loop earns its cost over a deterministic workflow. The answer is settled not once for an entire application but at each decision point, by measuring the cost per accepted task under a fixed contract. A model should direct the next action only where interpreting dynamic, unstructured evidence improves the task acceptance rate by a larger factor than the added inference calls increase the cost of an attempt. Deterministic software should govern everywhere else. Evaluated by this metric, dynamic model loops can earn their cost at phases such as root-cause diagnosis, where the next diagnostic transition cannot be enumerated in advance, while deterministic control structures manage the predictable orchestration surrounding them. The incident below supplies a cost threshold for that comparison. Its price, worked out in @sec-vol3-envelope-four-questions, shows the model calls to be a small fraction of one remediation attempt's cost. Whether additional diagnostic calls earn that cost depends on the relative acceptance improvement measured against a matched baseline under the same contract and latency constraints.

The second question asked what operational machinery must surround the model. The answer scales with the task's exposure to state, authority, and horizon. Managing state requires selectively retrieved context, explicitly budgeted serving state, and durable audit records that preserve source authority. Governing authority demands typed, mediated action interfaces, definitive effect settlement before any retry loop can execute, and process containment enforced within the execution substrate beneath the model. Managing horizon requires a supervisory harness that bounds the total trajectory, a write-ahead log of intent recorded before committing each external side effect, and compensating workflows capable of mitigating actions that cannot be reversed. A read-only lookup requires little of this protective scaffolding, whereas an autonomous remediation agent operating on live production systems demands all of it.

The third question asked how operators verify that a task has actually succeeded. The answer requires objective evidence collected from an authoritative endpoint that directly monitors the target system, evaluated against an explicit contract adopted by system owners before execution began. This verification must satisfy a pre-declared closure evidence level, with any residual uncertainty explicitly quantified and assigned to an accountable owner. A model's self-generated report never serves as evidence, however coherent or persuasive, because a component executing within the loop cannot certify its own output. Stated as an operational acceptance rule, this is the discipline of invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}).

Each answer is straightforward to state for an isolated component; agentic architectures fail most often where the answers must hold across subsystem boundaries, because individually tested services can drop an in-flight task when state, authority, and verification pass between them. The answers are therefore tested on one complete incident handled by the remediation agent, the lighthouse that exercises horizon, state, and authority at once, followed from its contract across the memory and execution boundaries to the one boundary no runtime can close on the owner's behalf.

## One Incident Through the System {#sec-vol3-conclusion-capstone}

A database service triggers a query-latency alert shortly after a configuration change. An automated remediation agent inspects telemetry, correlates logs, and proposes reverting to the previous known-good settings. The human operator approves the rollback, but the configuration endpoint drops the network connection before returning an acknowledgment. Whether the mutation took effect is now unknown, the classic dilemma of a lost acknowledgment in a distributed system, and no fluent explanation from a language model can resolve it. If the runtime interprets the timeout as a failure and retries under a fresh operation identifier, it risks executing the mutation twice. If it optimistically assumes success, it risks closing an incident while degraded queries continue to impact production. If it simply halts, it leaves a live production change in an unverified state with no entity accountable for it. Each failure mode arises by default when every component satisfies its local contract and no component owns the boundary between them. The end-to-end argument that grounded the closure evidence levels (@sec-vol3-intro-invariant-closure) applies to this single incident. An intermediate success report from a tool or a model call cannot establish acceptance, and only the principal holding the task contract can verify completion against direct evidence from the service.\index{End-to-end argument!task acceptance}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_hsa.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with all three axes, Horizon, State, and Authority, highlighted in purple."}

*Horizon, state, and authority return together, and the runtime closes each on one trajectory.*
:::

This incident, `incident_42` on database service `db_primary_01`, is a workload of the remediation agent (@sec-vol3-intro-lighthouses), the book's irreversible actor, which operates over a bounded horizon, mutates shared production state, and exercises real authority over a live service. Its single trajectory, from diagnostic telemetry through operator approval, dispatch, and acceptance, anchors the rest of the chapter. At every transition the criterion is the same. The system must durably and verifiably record what it proposed, what permissions were granted, what effects occurred, what evidence validates the outcome, and which principal bears ongoing responsibility. In this architecture, the managed database service owns its active configuration, the runtime orchestrator owns execution and control decisions, and the accepting authority verifies whether post-remediation evidence satisfies the delegated operational contract. One named human principal, `operations_owner_42`, is accountable both for any operation the runtime cannot settle and for the service once the incident is accepted. The runtime's settlement process, a runtime component rather than a person, reconciles uncertain operations on that owner's behalf.

### Trajectory ownership {#sec-vol3-conclusion-trajectory-owners}

The incident lifecycle begins under `incident_contract_v1`, which grants bounded diagnostic read access and sets gates for proposing, approving, and validating configuration mutations. Initial privileges are observational only. The runtime provisions `read_scope_42` to query authorized service endpoints, ensuring that telemetry gathering cannot inadvertently trigger state changes or be coerced into production writes. Throughout this trace, identifiers such as `read_scope_42` denote durable local record keys rather than opaque cryptographic hashes.

Next, the context manager gathers the initial latency alert, recent time-series metrics, active configuration parameters, and relevant runbook sections into an auditable manifest, `context_manifest_42`. Every observation in this manifest records its originating source, a version tag when available, and a precise ingestion timestamp. The retrieved runbook suggests a memory-pool misconfiguration, but it might describe a previous software deployment. By diffing the runbook recommendations against the active production configuration (`config_v7`) and current telemetry, the agent formulates a diagnostic hypothesis. Additional diagnostic queries, constrained by the task's remaining call budget, must corroborate this hypothesis against alternative explanations such as downstream network congestion or disk saturation.

When the diagnostic evidence converges on a known regression, the model emits `change_request_42`, which specifies the target configuration keys, the desired values, and the expected baseline version `config_v7`. In accordance with incident change policy, an authorized human operator reviews the proposed diff and issues `approval_42`. This record binds the operator's identity to the request identifier, the target host, the exact payload parameters, the prerequisite baseline `config_v7`, and an expiration window. The approval records permission for that exact payload and nothing broader; it does not perform the mutation. The model drafts the operational rationale, but it cannot grant itself execution authority. An approval granted minutes before execution is an earlier authorization check, and complete mediation (definition \ref{dfn-complete-mediation}) requires a fresh one at the moment of use.\index{Complete mediation!action gate} Prior to network dispatch, the runtime action gate therefore rechecks operator authorization, compares the payload against the approval's digest, inspects the expiration deadline, confirms resource quotas, and evaluates runtime preconditions. If an operator revokes the ticket or the model generates an altered proposal, the original approval no longer matches and cannot silently apply to a mutated repair payload.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Rechecking an approved request's digest, expiry, budget, and authorization at the dispatch boundary is established in @sec-vol3-agent-harness-dispatch-rechecks.
:::

Even a thorough pre-dispatch check leaves a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race if a peer operator changes the settings between the gate check and the write. The endpoint closes this window with the conditional update of @sec-vol3-tool-calling-conditional-updates, an atomic expected-version check that applies the change only if the live version still matches `config_v7` and otherwise rejects it, returning the task for re-diagnosis.\index{Optimistic concurrency control!expected-version check} The endpoint also makes the write idempotent in the sense of definition \ref{dfn-idempotent-action}: it deduplicates requests by an operation identity bound to the caller, target, and payload, and retains that identity across a window longer than the maximum client retry horizon, so a replayed request inside the window is recognized rather than reapplied.\index{Idempotency!operation identity} A read-only operation-status lookup completes the endpoint contract. These guarantees must live in the endpoint itself, since a client tool schema can declare an invariant but only the server can enforce it. Before transmitting the RPC, the runtime appends an intent record for `op_42` to a write-ahead journal at the durability boundary chosen for the deployment, together with its *recovery descriptor*: the obligation registration of the trajectory saga, here the corrective-action template, the preconditions it must satisfy, and the accountable owner, `operations_owner_42`. Once both are persistent on disk, the runtime dispatches the request with operation identity `op_42` and expected version `config_v7`.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Deduplication by an operation identity bound to caller, target, and payload is established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-operation-ids.
:::

The endpoint's response is then lost in transit, and the runtime sees a socket timeout. This is the lost-acknowledgment problem that opened @sec-vol3-failure-recovery-introduction, and the timeout yields no information about execution state. The network may have dropped the outbound packet, the endpoint may still be executing the transaction, or the endpoint may have committed the write and lost the acknowledgment on the way back. Instead of retrying blindly or declaring failure, the runtime logs the status of `op_42` as unknown and hands it to the settlement process, which issues an authorized status query against the endpoint's operation registry rather than a second mutating RPC. In the successful branch of this scenario, the lookup confirms that `op_42` committed the requested payload, transitioning the database configuration to `config_v8`. The immutable operation identity binds this remote confirmation to the local dispatch record, resolving the ambiguity even if the original RPC was delayed in transit. If the lookup instead returns an empty record or meets a transient outage, the settlement process cannot conclude that the mutation failed, because the original request might still be queued in the network. In that branch the status stays unknown, preserved through the recovery descriptor as an open obligation of `operations_owner_42` rather than lost when the process terminates.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Registering the recovery obligation alongside the forward intent, before dispatch, is established in @sec-vol3-failure-recovery-obligation-registration.
:::

Confirming that `config_v8` committed settles the mutation but not the incident. The context manager retires the stale `config_v7` snapshot and assembles fresh telemetry under live load. Assume that latency percentiles and error budgets over an observation window, `health_window_42`, meet the thresholds in `incident_contract_v1` and that the policy checks pass. An authorized principal or automated gatekeeper then signs `acceptance_42`, which binds together the original incident contract, the operator approval, the settled operation identifier, the new active configuration version (`config_v8`), and the validated metric window. Only then is the incident formally closed under contract for the evaluated duration. Monitoring the service after the window passes to `operations_owner_42`, the same owner who would have held `op_42` had its status stayed unknown.

Seen from above, this one incident has crossed nearly every part of the book (@fig-vol3-trajectory-lifecycle). The adopted contract came first; the loop that diagnosed the regression was assembled from the model call, context, tools, and sandbox of Parts I to III; the harness of Part IV wrapped every step; and acceptance rested on external evidence rather than the agent's report. Learning and delegation never entered, because neither was needed to close this task.

::: {#fig-vol3-trajectory-lifecycle fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**One Trajectory Through the Whole System**: A task contract, defined in the introduction and adopted at the specification boundary that Part VII closes on, governs a live loop in which context assembly (Part II) feeds a model call (Part I) whose proposal becomes a validated, authorized tool call run in a sandbox (Part III), with the observation returning to context as data. The harness (Part IV) wraps every step with budgets, the approval gate, the durable log, and recovery. Acceptance rests on scoped external evidence rather than the agent's report; learning (Part V) and scale (Part VI) are optional lifecycle choices." fig-alt="Layered diagram. A slate box at the top labeled Task contract, adopted by an authorized owner, Part VII, points down with an arrow labeled governs into a purple container labeled Harness around every step, Part IV, with the sublabel budgets, approval gate, durable log, recovery. Inside the container four stages form a clockwise loop: Context assembly (Part II) to Model call (Part I), down via proposal to Tool call (Part III), left to Sandbox (Part III), and a dashed arrow back up to Context assembly labeled observation as data. A small purple checkpoint mark sits on each of the four loop arrows. An arrow labeled settled outcome leads from the container down to a slate Acceptance box, Part IV, reading scoped evidence, not the agent's report. A dashed line labeled checked against runs from the task contract around the right side to the acceptance box. Below, a dashed arrow labeled if chosen leads to a pale dashed Learning box (Part V, optional, across tasks), beside a pale dashed Scale box (Part VI, optional, across agents)."}
![](images/svg/capstone_trajectory_owners.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The audit chain summarized in @tbl-vol3-capstone-owners enables an independent auditor or site reliability engineer to reconstruct the causal lineage of the incident without relying on a language model's retrospective self-report. Structured records also expose gaps at once. A successful completion token from a model call cannot settle the network status of `op_42`, and an unanchored telemetry snapshot lacking a verified observation window cannot validate an acceptance claim.

| **Transition**                 | **Owner**                                          | **Record it leaves**                                                                     |
|:-------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Task admitted                  | Runtime under the delegated contract               | `incident_42`, `incident_contract_v1`, limits, and `read_scope_42`                       |
| Evidence selected              | Context manager and diagnostic tools               | `context_manifest_42` with source, version, time, and omissions                          |
| Change proposed and approved   | Model proposes; authorized operator decides        | `change_request_42` and its bound `approval_42`                                          |
| Change admitted and dispatched | Runtime action gate and operation journal          | Durable `op_42` intent, recovery descriptor, and dispatch record                         |
| Lost response reconciled       | Settlement process for `operations_owner_42`       | Source outcome for `op_42`, confirming `config_v8` or preserving uncertainty             |
| Incident accepted              | Designated accepting principal with runtime checks | `acceptance_42`, `health_window_42`, and residual duty assigned to `operations_owner_42` |

: **Owners and Records Along One Trajectory**: The incident's consequential transitions remain auditable through explicit owners and linked records. An unresolved outcome remains a recorded obligation rather than disappearing when execution stops. {#tbl-vol3-capstone-owners tbl-colwidths="[28,34,38]"}

### Adversarial evidence within the same task {#sec-vol3-conclusion-adversarial-evidence}

Real production telemetry is rarely sterile. A diagnostic log entry or an issue tracker comment can carry an indirect prompt injection, instructions written to exfiltrate database credentials to an external server. The payload enters the agent's context through an authorized diagnostic read, yet the untrusted text inherits none of the operator's administrative authority; an agent that acted on it would be the confused deputy of definition \ref{dfn-confused-deputy}, spending the operator's grant on the attacker's intent.\index{Confused deputy!prompt injection} While structured provenance tagging and XML delimiters assist the model in distinguishing ingested data from operational instructions, model-level comprehension provides no security boundary. Strong isolation outside the model runtime must govern what an ostensibly schema-valid tool call can execute using legitimate system privileges.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Indirect prompt injection, delivered through an observation the agent reads rather than by the interacting user, is established in @sec-vol3-security-injection-entry-points.
:::

In this incident scenario, an attempted exfiltration collides with layered architectural barriers. If the manipulated model emits a tool call directed to an unauthorized external IP address, the runtime action gate blocks dispatch, because `read_scope_42` grants queries only against the named diagnostic endpoints and an arbitrary address is not among them. Independently of that grant, the sandbox's egress policy drops unsanctioned outbound sockets at the network layer regardless of what code or parameters the agent generates. The read grant says which services the task may ask; the egress policy says which hosts any process may reach. Allowing unrestricted outbound connections would create an exfiltration channel even with local filesystems mounted read-only.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Network egress enforcement placed outside the guest's control boundary is established in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-egress-enforcement.
:::

The harder case uses only permitted operations. A diagnostic query to an endpoint inside `read_scope_42` can carry a database connection string in one of its arguments, and both the tool and the destination are allowed. The dispatch release check of @eq-vol3-flow-dispatch catches it. The credential carries a confidentiality label whose recipient set excludes the telemetry service, the label propagates into the query string built from it, and the reference monitor rejects dispatch because the recipient is not in that set. Layered constraints thus bound the blast radius of a successful injection, at the gate, at the network layer, and on the data itself.

When the action gate intercepts an unauthorized or malformed action, it appends the rejection to the audit journal as an undispatched intent. An operation that has already crossed into production is a different matter, because terminating the sandbox does not undo an external state change; `operations_owner_42` must determine from the audit log which side effects materialized and select the compensating action. If an adversarial prompt leads the model to assert that latency has normalized, the runtime ignores the assertion, since model output never substitutes for telemetry verified across `health_window_42`. The same ownership boundaries that handle component outages handle adversarial attacks.

The remediation trajectory terminates with a single model and a single runtime controller. Mining the trace for post-training or delegating sub-problems to sub-agents are later, optional decisions (@sec-vol3-conclusion-seams, @sec-vol3-conclusion-adaptation). Neither optimization alters the authorization invariants required to dispatch `op_42` or the empirical evidence demanded to seal `acceptance_42`.

### The principle table {#sec-vol3-conclusion-principle-table}

Managing `incident_42` draws on responsibilities established across separate chapters. The context window must represent the live configuration, operator approval must bind the exact mutation, and acceptance must verify the operation that actually committed on the remote service. No single mechanism guarantees all three. @Tbl-vol3-principle-table collects the fifteen principles of the book into one reference, each with its governing equation or structural contract and the design consequence it predicts.

The three H·S·A exposures organize the table. Part I prices an isolated model call and states the statistical limits of verification. Parts II, III, and IV build closure for the three exposures a single call cannot manage on its own: state carried across turns, authority over external systems, and a horizon over which errors compound. Part V changes the policy weights without expanding authority, since fine-tuning alters which trajectories the model proposes but grants no new access. Part VI multiplies all three exposures across sub-agents. Invariant closure anchors the table, because it marks the one thing computation cannot certify for itself, the task contract that defines acceptance. The exposures also interact; persisting state over a long horizon requires durable write-ahead logging, and delegation carries state and authority across agent boundaries.

|:-----------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:-------------|:------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

| \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-goodput}        | Trajectory goodput and the accepted task         | VI           | All three, priced       | $\CostPerAcceptedTask=\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability$; $\ConcurrentTrajectories=\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\,\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryDuration]$ per resource                                                                                                                                                                                 | Raising acceptance can cut cost more than cheaper tokens; long tool waits raise held sandboxes in proportion, and the mean alone does not give deadline capacity                                                                        |

: **Fifteen Principles and What They Predict**: Each principle appears in its teaching home with the H·S·A exposure it primarily addresses, its core equation or governing statement, and the design consequence that form predicts. Symbols carry the meanings given where each equation is derived. The exposure column is a lens rather than a partition, and each prediction holds under the assumptions its owning chapter states. {#tbl-vol3-principle-table tbl-colwidths="[4,14,7,8,40,27]"}

These invariants bound every performance optimization. KV cache prefix reuse saves the same compute whether or not the cached text still describes the live service, so a reused prefix holding a stale diagnostic snapshot is cheap and wrong at once; freshness has to come from the source's read or version contract, never from the cache. A smaller, faster model has economic value only if its acceptance rate and tail latency still meet the service level objective. Post-training and delegation remain elective interventions, justified only by matched comparison and cost-per-accepted-task accounting.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Cost per accepted task, measured under a declared contract, checker, and environment, as the unit for comparing configurations is established in @sec-vol3-agent-economics-accounting.
:::

::: {#chk-19-principle-table .callout-checkpoint title="Reading the principle table as a design tool"}

The equations in the principle table provide concrete quantitative estimates for sizing and evaluating real architectures rather than theoretical abstractions.

- [ ] **Horizon budget**: Using @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding, what per-step violation rate keeps the chance of any unchecked violation over $\TurnHorizon$ turns below a target violation probability, and how must that rate change when $\TurnHorizon$ doubles?
- [ ] **Acceptance vs. price**: By @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task, compare cutting the cost per attempt by a fraction $\RelativeImprovementFraction$ with raising acceptance by the same relative fraction. Which lowers cost per accepted task more, and why does a token discount that touches only part of the attempt cost lose ground to the acceptance gain?
- [ ] **Pass rate vs. acceptance**: A change raises the verifier's pass rate but leaves acceptance under protected checks unchanged. Which two rows of the principle table explain why cost per accepted task does not fall?

:::

The principle table states what each mechanism guarantees in general. The incident still needs those guarantees written down as the specific terms it runs under: which outcome counts as recovery, which actions are permitted and when, and which evidence closes the task. That is the job of the incident's task contract.

## Workload Contract Specification {#sec-vol3-conclusion-envelope}

When the latency alert fires for `incident_42`, the runtime starts a diagnostic workflow, not an open-ended authorization to modify the production database. An unconstrained loop could restore query throughput by disabling secondary index updates or relaxing integrity constraints, trading durability for speed. The deployment therefore grounds the workflow in `incident_contract_v1`, an adopted task contract that separates the desired service outcome from the mechanisms an agent may use to reach it.

### The incident's five-part contract {#sec-vol3-envelope-contract-formalism}

Before dispatching any diagnostic query or rollback on `db_primary_01`, the runtime must know which settings may change, which endpoints may be read, and which metric window closes the ticket. The five contract components bind `incident_42` to an identified service, explicit permission boundaries, and named decision authorities (@tbl-vol3-contract-decomposition).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The five-part task contract governing an agentic workload is established in @sec-vol3-intro-five-part-contract.
:::

| Contract field                                   | Incident-specific commitment                                                                                                                                    | Owner or supporting record                                               |
|:-------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Goal, $\TaskContractGoal$                        | Restore acceptable query latency for `db_primary_01` without violating the required error-rate and change-policy conditions; leave unrelated settings unchanged | `incident_contract_v1`, adopted by the authorized task owner             |
| Environment, $\TaskEnvironment$                  | Operate on the identified live service; treat `config_v7` as the expected baseline, not as a promise that the service remains unchanged                         | Configuration source and its versioned operation interface               |
| Permitted actions, $\PermittedActions$           | Initially perform diagnostics under `read_scope_42`; apply the exact proposed settings only after the required current approval and dispatch checks             | `change_request_42`, `approval_42`, and the runtime's action gate        |
| Available observations, $\AvailableObservations$ | Return authorized, bounded diagnostic results with source, version, capture time, and omission information                                                      | Tool result records and `context_manifest_42`                            |
| Completion criteria, $\CompletionCriteria$       | Confirm the authorized operation's outcome, the required service metrics over the stated window, and the applicable change-policy checks                        | `op_42`, `health_window_42`, and the adopted decision in `acceptance_42` |

: **The Incident Contract**: The same five components connect this delegated task directly to its operational permissions, evidence records, and accountable owners. Merely identifying a record name does not establish that its underlying validation checks have passed. {#tbl-vol3-contract-decomposition tbl-colwidths="[23,48,29]"}

The goal encodes process constraints alongside target metrics because the validity of an outcome depends on how the system reaches it. Here that dependency takes the form of approval bindings and version preconditions, and the contract places the preconditions at the infrastructure layer. A configuration endpoint without an atomic expected-version check cannot safely host this workflow, however often the runtime re-reads `config_v7`, because a concurrent write can slip between the final read and the update. Observation bounds constrain diagnostics just as strictly. Under `read_scope_42` the agent may query telemetry from designated endpoints but not customer rows, payload logs, or external destinations, and tool output arrives truncated and flagged, with the full output in a separate log sink. Heuristic filters that strip known keys cannot prove an output free of sensitive data or injected instructions, so protection rests on structural boundaries over what the agent reads, where context flows, and which endpoints receive its output.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Head-and-tail byte budgets and explicit truncation notices for tool output are established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-bounded-capture.
:::

### Exposures and envelope bounds {#sec-vol3-envelope-four-questions}

The introduction placed the remediation agent at a horizon of tens of turns, mutable shared production state ($\StateExposureLevel_3$), and changes that cannot always be compensated ($\AuthorityExposureLevel_3$), and `incident_42` sits exactly there. Each exposure sets an obligation. Diagnosis needs finite allowances for model and tool calls, live service state needs source-aware tracking, and the step from diagnostic reads to a production change needs an explicit escalation of authority. The envelope attached to `incident_contract_v1` applies the harness's trajectory budgets: caps on turns, wall-clock time, observation size, disk, and spend, with the liability of each admitted call reserved in advance and a reserve kept for the health check and recovery.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Multi-dimensional budget vectors and the advance reservation of each admitted call's liability are established in @sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-conclusion-incident-price
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRICE OF ONE INCIDENT_42 ATTEMPT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The envelope paragraph of @sec-vol3-envelope-four-questions.
# │ Goal: Put the capstone incident on the same account as every lighthouse.
# │ Show: Horizon, attempt cost by term, model and approval shares, cost per
# │       accepted task, time to mitigate, and the expected loss of a wrong
# │       change written with no check ahead of it.
# │ How:  C_eff = E[C_attempt] / p_acc; L_A = p_bad * consequence * (1 - rho)
# │       with rho = 0.
# │ Note: Agents.Remediation.OnCall workload profile (teaching assumptions,
# │       not measured incident data), the profile Agent Economics prices for
# │       this lighthouse.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Agents, USD
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_usd

class IncidentPrice:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Registry workload profile) ──────────────────────────────
    remed = Agents.Remediation.OnCall
    turns = remed.horizon_turns
    c_model = remed.model_cost_per_attempt.to(USD).magnitude  # model calls
    c_env = remed.environment_cost_per_attempt.to(USD).magnitude  # telemetry queries, change tools
    c_assess = remed.assessment_cost_per_attempt.to(USD).magnitude  # health-window check
    c_approval = remed.approval_cost_per_attempt.to(USD).magnitude  # reviewer time x hourly rate
    p_acc = remed.acceptance_probability
    t_diag = remed.diagnosis_time.to("minute").magnitude
    t_approve = remed.approval_decision_time.to("minute").magnitude
    t_apply = remed.apply_verify_time.to("minute").magnitude
    p_bad = remed.wrong_change_probability
    impact = remed.wrong_change_impact.to(USD).magnitude

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    c_attempt = c_model + c_env + c_assess + c_approval
    c_eff = c_attempt / p_acc
    model_share = c_model / c_attempt
    approval_share = c_approval / c_attempt
    t_total = t_diag + t_approve + t_apply
    approve_time_share = t_approve / t_total
    diag_time_share = t_diag / t_total
    loss_unchecked = p_bad * impact * (1 - 0)
    loss_vs_attempt = loss_unchecked / c_attempt

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants the prose relies on) ───────────────────────
    check(model_share < 0.01, "Prose says model calls are under one percent of the attempt")
    check(approval_share > 0.9, "Prose says approval dominates the attempt cost")
    check(abs(approve_time_share - 0.5) < 1e-9, "Prose says approval is half the time to mitigate")
    check(diag_time_share < approve_time_share, "Prose says diagnosis is a smaller share of time than approval")
    check(loss_vs_attempt > 20, "Prose says the unchecked loss is over twenty attempts' worth")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    turns_str = fmt_int(turns)
    c_model_str = fmt_usd(c_model, precision=2)
    c_env_str = fmt_usd(c_env, precision=2)
    c_assess_str = fmt_usd(c_assess, precision=2)
    c_approval_str = fmt_usd(c_approval, precision=0)
    c_attempt_str = fmt_usd(c_attempt, precision=2)
    p_acc_str = fmt_percent(p_acc, precision=0, style="prose")
    c_eff_str = fmt_usd(c_eff, precision=2)
    model_share_str = fmt_percent(model_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    approval_share_str = fmt_percent(approval_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    t_total_str = fmt_int(round(t_total))
    approve_time_share_str = fmt_percent(approve_time_share, precision=0, style="prose")
    diag_time_share_str = fmt_percent(diag_time_share, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_bad_str = fmt_percent(p_bad, precision=0, style="prose")
    impact_str = fmt_usd(impact, precision=0)
    loss_unchecked_str = fmt_usd(loss_unchecked, precision=0)
    loss_vs_attempt_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(loss_vs_attempt), precision=0)
```

Priced on the remediation workload profile used for this lighthouse in @sec-vol3-agent-economics-synthesis, one `incident_42` attempt runs about `{python} IncidentPrice.turns_str` turns and costs `{python} IncidentPrice.c_attempt_str`: `{python} IncidentPrice.c_model_str` of model calls, `{python} IncidentPrice.c_env_str` of telemetry queries and change tools, `{python} IncidentPrice.c_assess_str` for the health-window check, and `{python} IncidentPrice.c_approval_str` of on-call review for the approval. At `{python} IncidentPrice.p_acc_str` acceptance, each accepted incident costs `{python} IncidentPrice.c_eff_str` (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task). The model accounts for `{python} IncidentPrice.model_share_str` of the attempt, while operator approval takes `{python} IncidentPrice.approval_share_str` of the money and `{python} IncidentPrice.approve_time_share_str` of the `{python} IncidentPrice.t_total_str`-minute time to mitigate. This profile sets a threshold for additional diagnosis rather than establishing superiority over a fixed workflow. If all other expected attempt costs remain unchanged, doubling the model-call charges raises attempt cost by its existing model share, `{python} IncidentPrice.model_share_str`. The added calls lower cost per accepted task only if acceptance rises by a greater relative fraction under the same contract and latency limits; that gain must be measured.

The same profile shows where the danger lies. A wrong change, proposed in `{python} IncidentPrice.p_bad_str` of attempts and costing `{python} IncidentPrice.impact_str` when it fully commits, carries an expected irreversible loss of `{python} IncidentPrice.loss_unchecked_str` per attempt if no check stands ahead of the write (@eq-vol3-expected-irreversible-loss), about `{python} IncidentPrice.loss_vs_attempt_mult_str` the cost of the attempt itself. For this workload, then, the envelope's caps on turns and spend matter less than its gates: the approval binding, the expected-version check, and the health window that bounds how long a wrong change runs before anyone reverses it.

The contract also makes idempotency, request deduplication, and an operation-status lookup prerequisites for admitting any remediation workload, so that a timeout leads the runtime to ask the endpoint for the operation's state rather than issue a duplicate mutation (@sec-vol3-conclusion-execution).

### Operating-envelope decisions {#sec-vol3-envelope-boundaries}

Suppose the run reaches its deadline while the status of `op_42` is still being reconciled. Extending the deadline because the model predicts imminent success violates the envelope, and marking the operation failed fabricates an unverified outcome. The runtime instead halts further admission, logs the expiration, and preserves the pending operation identifier with its reconciliation quota, while `operations_owner_42` remains responsible for the orphaned operation. Staying within the turn and token limits proves nothing about recovery either, because resource accounting and acceptance are separate boundaries. Mutating the service, verifying its health, and closing the ticket are distinct milestones with separate evidence. Sizing the envelope is a trade-off of its own. Tighter ceilings shrink the blast radius but can make the completion criteria unattainable, and looser ones grant latitude at the price of liability that needs human oversight.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ A worksheet mapping each contract condition to its design obligation and the evidence to record is developed in @sec-vol3-app-ref-arch-profiles.
:::

## State and Evidence Across Boundaries {#sec-vol3-conclusion-memory}

Before the mitigation, `context_manifest_42` selects diagnostic evidence describing `config_v7`. Once the endpoint confirms that `op_42` applied `config_v8`, any prompt that still presents `config_v7` as active state gives the model an incorrect basis for its next decision. The earlier observation remains true, but its role has changed; it no longer describes the live system and serves instead as historical evidence of the trajectory.

### Evidence refresh and cached computation {#sec-vol3-memory-coherence-invalidation}

When `op_42` updates `db_primary_01` from `config_v7` to `config_v8`, a cached summary or vector index that still reports `config_v7` misleads the next turn even though the KV cache for the old prompt tokens remains mathematically valid. To keep those guarantees separate, the incident's records occupy distinct roles in an evidence chain. The configuration service is the *source record*, the runtime operation log is the *event log* of decisions, approvals, and settlement status, model-written incident summaries are *agent-written memory*, and diagnostic vector indices are *derived retrieval indexes*. The context manifest is none of these; it is the working-context view assembled for the next model call. No derived role can override the source, and the operation log attests only to the events it durably wrote, not to an external effect it has not verified (@sec-vol3-persistence-event-sourcing).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Source records, event logs, agent-written memory, and derived indexes as roles in an evidence chain are established in @sec-vol3-long-term-memory-record-roles.
:::

When the source confirms `config_v8`, context assembly updates the active configuration entry, keeps the `config_v7` record only where it justifies the remediation step, and invalidates derived artifacts that depend on the superseded version, such as diagnostic summaries and precomputed runbook excerpts. If the retrieval index lags, the runtime issues an authorized direct read, and if no read is possible the manifest records the omission rather than presenting stale data as current.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Withdrawing a staged observation's authority over current state when its source changes is established in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot.
:::

The serving system judges validity by a different rule. KV cache tensors computed for tokens describing `config_v7` remain valid representations of those tokens whatever the service now holds, so substituting `config_v8` evidence ends prefix reuse at the first changed token and leaves the unchanged prefix reusable. Prefix coherence (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}) governs computational reuse and source authority (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}) governs semantic freshness, and a cache hit establishes only the first. Freshness checks at prompt time also cannot freeze the service while the model deliberates, which is why the endpoint's expected-version check at application remains the final guard.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Reuse of KV state only over an exact token prefix computed under the same weights and execution parameters is established in @sec-vol3-kv-cache-prefix-compatibility.
:::

Provenance follows the same separation. The runtime records which endpoint supplied each observation under `read_scope_42`, its timestamp and version, any filtering applied, and the model request that consumed it, and these host-verified events stay distinct from the model's hypotheses about the cause of the alert. Text read from a trusted store, including an instruction injected into a log stream, gains no authority by being stored there. Permissions are evaluated against capability grants, and observed data remains passive payload.

### Cross-subsystem seams and ownership {#sec-vol3-conclusion-seams}

In the source-to-context example, storage and serving each operate within their local specifications while the agent as a whole acts on stale evidence. That failure pattern recurs at every subsystem boundary the incident crosses. @Tbl-vol3-seams names five such seams, the last two of which arise only if the deployment adds learning or delegation.

| Seam                                     | Incident-specific failure                                                                                       | Principles that meet here                                                                                                                               | Owner and required record                                                                                                                                                 |
|:-----------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| World and its representations            | `config_v7` is presented as current after `config_v8` is confirmed                                              | Source authority (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}) against prefix reuse (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence})                           | Context and retrieval owners preserve source/version bindings in `context_manifest_42`; the action endpoint enforces the expected version when applying a change          |
| Proposal to effect                       | A lost reply is treated as failure, leading to an unsafe repeat of `op_42`                                      | Intent before effect (principle \ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}), then settlement before retry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement})   | The settlement process and `operations_owner_42` retain the admitted intent, operation identity, and unresolved status until the endpoint supplies outcome evidence       |
| Recovery and authority                   | A recorded recovery plan is treated as permission to apply a corrective change to a now-different service       | Intent before effect (principle \ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}) against the typed action contract (principle \ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi})     | `operations_owner_42` retains the descriptor and residual duty; any corrective action needs current authorization and applicable preconditions                            |
| Recorded incident to learning, if chosen | Acceptance of the incident makes every step a training target, or the release grader becomes a selection reward | Release evidence (principle \ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}) against the verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry})       | Curation and evaluation owners separately admit any training record derived from the incident, keep its permitted use and evidence limits, and protect release evaluation |
| Across workers, if delegated             | Diagnostic workers duplicate a consumable allowance or their agreement is treated as independent confirmation   | Coordination tax (principle \ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}) against trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}) | Delegating runtime records scoped assignments and reservations; the integration owner checks returned evidence and retains unresolved child obligations                   |

: **Incident seams, principles, and owners**: Each boundary needs both an owner and a record that preserves the distinction the next subsystem relies on, and at each one two principles meet or pull against each other. Local success alone does not establish the end-to-end task result. {#tbl-vol3-seams tbl-colwidths="[15,25,24,36]"}

Delegation makes the final row concrete without changing the acceptance contract. A worker may receive a subset of `read_scope_42`, a reusable capability, but a consumable allowance cannot be copied the same way; concurrent workers reserve against one shared budget rather than each receiving an independently spendable quota (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}). Agreement among diagnostic workers also cannot substitute for verification, because workers that read the same noisy inputs or each other's intermediate results fail together. Whether delegation pays at all is weighed against the coordination tax (principle \ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}) in @sec-vol3-conclusion-adaptation.

With these records in place, an auditor can reconstruct what the runtime observed, what it proposed, what authority it held, and what state the external world committed. Turning that evidence into an admissible next action, whether settling an ambiguous request or dispatching a compensating repair, falls to the execution and recovery boundary.

## Execution Harness Synthesis {#sec-vol3-conclusion-execution}

The capstone trace resolved its lost reply with a single status query, and it could do so only because every piece of state that query needed was persisted before the network dropped the reply. Three properties made each step admissible: durability that covers the declared failure domain, evidence states the runtime keeps apart, and obligations that outlive the process that created them.

### Durable intent before dispatch {#sec-vol3-execution-pipeline-stages}

The trace wrote the intent for `op_42` and its recovery descriptor before the request left (principle \ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}), binding the operation to its request, approval, endpoint contract, reservation, and accountable owner. Registering the descriptor only after a response would have left exactly the gap the lost reply exposed, an active remote mutation with no durable record of who must reconcile it. The ordering is a database write-ahead log applied to an external effect, with one difference that shapes everything after it. A database's recovery manager can redo or undo a logged update itself, whereas the runtime can neither redo nor undo the endpoint's mutation; the log tells it which operation to ask about, and only the endpoint can answer.\index{Write-ahead logging!intent record} The acknowledgment must also cover the declared failure domain, since a local `fsync` does not survive the loss of the storage device, and the execution gate withholds dispatch when that acknowledgment is missing or ambiguous. Recording intent commits the system to track the operation, not to execute it, so a pause or a revoked authority can still withhold the unsent request.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Durable intent, the admitted operation acknowledged by storage that survives the declared failure domain before dispatch, is established in @sec-vol3-persistence-wal.
:::

### Lost responses and unresolved operations {#sec-vol3-execution-sagas}

Neither the expired timer nor the surviving intent log can say which of the trace's three outcomes occurred. Because the agent's local log and the external configuration service cannot share one atomic transaction, recovery from a lost reply depends on guarantees at the endpoint, and issuing an idempotent status query rather than a fresh mutation is settlement before retry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}). Once correlated evidence confirms that the endpoint applied `config_v8`, dependent tasks may consume the result, and any later replay of the same operation must conform to the endpoint's repeat contract and pass admission checks again. @Tbl-vol3-execution-pipeline-stages separates boundary states that naive agent architectures treat as interchangeable tool errors.

| Evidence at the boundary                                          | What the runtime may conclude                                               | Continuation and owner                                                                                           |
|:------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Current admission fails before this attempt is released           | This attempt was withheld through the gate; earlier attempts are unaffected | Record rejection and its reason; reconsider only under current authority                                         |
| `op_42` intent survives, but its response is lost                 | The external outcome remains unknown                                        | Withhold dependent mutation; `operations_owner_42` retains reconciliation and outstanding liability              |
| Correlated status evidence establishes application as `config_v8` | This operation's effect is established under the endpoint contract          | Record settlement evidence; obtain the service-health evidence required for acceptance                           |
| Status remains unavailable within the follow-up allowance         | Automated reconciliation has not established the outcome                    | End this continuation as unresolved; retain the operation, evidence, reservation, and acknowledged handoff owner |
: **Execution Evidence and Continuation**: Local rejection, uncertain delivery, and established application support different decisions. Closing a continuation does not close an unresolved external obligation. {#tbl-vol3-execution-pipeline-stages tbl-colwidths="[31,31,38]"}

Settling the operation does not complete acceptance, which still needs service-health evidence. The operation's budget reservation also stays open until settlement, because a charge for remote work can arrive after its reply, as the canceled child with a late bill showed in @sec-vol3-agent-economics-governance.

### Recovery and stopping obligations {#sec-vol3-execution-watchdog}

In `incident_42`, the configuration on `db_primary_01` is restorable selected state, since the endpoint keeps `config_v7` and a further versioned write can return to it, whereas the queries `db_primary_01` served while a wrong configuration was live are a commitment that cannot be undone, which is why the health window rather than a later rollback limits the damage of a wrong change. To separate those cases before any mutation leaves the harness, a recovery contract asks three things of every effect before dispatch: its target state, the recovery action available under the task's authority, and the evidence that would show recovery worked. Even a write that restores `config_v7` is, in the vocabulary of the trajectory saga (definition \ref{dfn-trajectory-saga}), a compensating step, a new forward action that observers may see half-applied rather than an erasure of the first.\index{Saga!compensating action} It needs current credentials, approval, and preconditions checked against the live service, the same admission the typed action contract (principle \ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}) applies to any forward action. Because `op_42` was itself a rollback, restoring `config_v7` would reinstate the configuration the incident was opened against, so the useful correction after a wrong `op_42` is usually a newly diagnosed change. Compensations can themselves stall or fail partially. Rolling back a local workspace cannot reverse an external configuration change, just as a network cancellation request cannot guarantee that the remote endpoint stopped executing. Until an authorized successor acknowledges the handoff, every residual obligation stays with `operations_owner_42`.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Restoring selected state, compensating a known effect, and managing a commitment that cannot be undone are established as recovery contracts in @sec-vol3-failure-recovery-recovery-contracts.
:::

Stopping a run must preserve admitted work in the same way. A semantic watchdog that halts a stalled loop can mistake legitimate polling of a pending status for a livelock, so the harness backs it with a hard dispatch ceiling. A hold then suspends new speculative dispatches, preserves every admitted operation, and lets only separately authorized settlement and recovery work proceed.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Semantic watchdogs that detect activity without progress are established in @sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs.
:::

::: {#chk-19-intervention-ladder .callout-checkpoint title="Auditing the incident's action boundary"}

Each prompt names a failure at the action boundary; decide which record or check must catch it.

- [ ] **Changed precondition**: `approval_42` names `config_v7`, but another operator changes the configuration before application. Which check must prevent the stale proposal from applying, and who may authorize a revised change?
- [ ] **Retry exposure**: The log contains the intent for `op_42`, but no response. If some fraction of lost replies hide an applied change, what fraction of fresh-identity retries duplicate the change, and which endpoint guarantee brings that fraction to zero?
- [ ] **Missing obligation**: A design records its recovery descriptor only after receiving success. Identify the failure interval this leaves uncovered and the record and owner that must survive it.
- [ ] **Unresolved exit**: The follow-up allowance expires while status remains unknown. Which operation, financial liability, and handoff records must remain even though this continuation ends?

:::

Because every failure in this trace is anchored to a defined boundary and an accountable owner, the record also shows where the next safeguard belongs. Choosing that safeguard is itself a decision that needs evidence.

## Evidence-Based Systems Intervention {#sec-vol3-conclusion-adaptation}

An execution trace supports a more precise question than whether the agent needs a larger model. If `context_manifest_42` still presents `config_v7` as current after settlement confirms `config_v8`, the defect lies in state selection. If the runtime blindly retries `op_42` after a timeout, the defect lies in outcome handling and the endpoint's recovery contract. Further training might change how often the model reaches these paths, but new weights cannot supply a missing state transition or make a non-idempotent retry safe.

Intervention selection\index{Intervention ladder!intervention selection} pairs an attributed failure with a targeted remedy, and the intervention ladder orders the candidates by cost and reversibility. Context and retrieval, tool interfaces, and runtime control come before changes to model weights, which are reserved for residual failures that evidence traces to the model's behavior rather than to a missing record or check. The ordering is a default justified by cost, not a sequence every failure must climb; an authorization bypass points directly to a runtime enforcement repair.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The intervention ladder ordering candidate remedies by operational cost and reversibility is established in @sec-vol3-flywheel-intervention-order.
:::

### Attribution and remedy selection {#sec-vol3-conclusion-remedy-selection}

Fine-tuning a model after a failed run of `incident_42` wastes training budget if the prompt omitted `config_v8` or the tool interface hid a pending operation behind a generic timeout. Because a trace records only what happened, isolating the responsible layer requires a counterfactual experiment. The engineer reconstructs the input, tool contract, runtime state, and outcome, then changes only the suspected cause. Supplying the missing configuration version in the prompt tests for an information deficit, and replacing an ambiguous timeout with an explicit pending status tests whether the tool interface misled the controller. A candidate fix is then evaluated across the affected task suite, with regression checks on unrelated workloads. @Tbl-vol3-intervention-ladder-tradeoffs pairs each kind of intervention with the evidence that justifies it: three reversible structural fixes, two training changes, and delegation, which is a separate architectural decision.

| Intervention           | Evidence motivating the change                                                                              | Obligation the change leaves in place                                                         |
|:-----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Context and retrieval  | Needed facts are absent, stale, or obscured in the actual model input                                       | Validate source versions and preserve current task constraints                                |
| Tool interface         | Arguments or outcome states are ambiguous to the caller                                                     | Enforce authorization and distinguish a rejected request from an unresolved effect            |
| Runtime control        | Budgets, action preconditions, or settlement rules are not enforced at the responsible boundary             | Test enforcement and recovery under the declared failure model                                |
| Supervised fine-tuning | Admitted demonstrations represent a recurring behavior the current policy handles poorly                    | Supply current contracts and evaluate generalization and regressions                          |
| Reward-driven learning | New attempts can be assessed under a useful scoped reward without a demonstrated response at every decision | Protect assessment, inspect reward gaps, and evaluate held-out behavior                       |
| Delegated trajectories | Separate ownership and focused contexts may improve a declared task objective                               | Bound authority and spending, reconcile results, and compare with a capable single controller |

: **Evidence for an Intervention**: A causal diagnosis directs the remedy; no row guarantees improvement or removes the obligations enforced elsewhere in the system. {#tbl-vol3-intervention-ladder-tradeoffs tbl-colwidths="[21,39,40]"}

Adapting model weights reshapes which actions the model proposes; it never relieves the runtime of enforcing contracts, budgets, or security boundaries. Supervised fine-tuning imitates demonstrated recovery paths, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards optimizes behavior through exploration. Both must show their gains on the deployment distribution, and a sandboxed reward evaluator can still be gamed or miss edge cases of the task.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Reward hacking, which exploits the gap between a verifiable reward and the intended task, is established in @sec-vol3-rlvr-score-intended-outcome.
:::

Delegation lies outside the ladder. Partitioning a task across agents changes topology, ownership boundaries, and communication overhead rather than repairing a failed component, and a workload with cleanly decoupled subtasks may warrant it without any training. The baseline is a capable single controller with selective retrieval and parallel tool calls, and the comparison must charge the redundant contexts, serialization across dependencies, and reconciliation that make up the coordination tax (principle \ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}). Diagnostic sub-agents reading logs in parallel could shorten triage for `incident_42`, with no worker permitted to apply production changes, but only if the serial share and integration overhead pass the screen of @eq-vol3-multiagent-speedup. Diagnosis takes only `{python} IncidentPrice.diag_time_share_str` of this incident's time to mitigate and approval takes `{python} IncidentPrice.approve_time_share_str`, so the screen is hard to pass, which is why `incident_42` closed without delegation.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Benchmarking a multi-agent design against a single controller with matched tools, budgets, and concurrency limits is established in @sec-vol3-multiagent-matched-conditions.
:::

An intervention that improves reliability must also pay for itself. A one-time investment in data, training, and evaluation is recovered only after enough tasks have run for the per-task saving to repay it (@eq-vol3-breakeven-volume), and the comparison holds only while both configurations accept the same share of tasks.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The break-even task volume of an adaptation investment is established in @sec-vol3-selection-adaptation-payback.
:::

Choosing an intervention therefore combines attribution, matched comparison, and end-to-end cost accounting, while authority and acceptance stay outside the configuration being changed. Once a remedy is chosen, the remaining question is what evidence supports releasing the changed configuration within its declared envelope.

## Empirical Safety Cases {#sec-vol3-conclusion-safety}

An incident record links an approved configuration change to an observed service outcome, but the link does not imply general correctness. The engineer must still establish which claims the record supports, which enforcement mechanisms make those claims trustworthy, and which failure modes remain unaddressed. The vehicle for that work is an empirical *safety case*, an inspectable, structured argument that specific claims hold within a defined operating envelope, as opposed to a certificate that the agent behaves correctly under all reachable conditions.[^fn-goal-structuring-notation]

[^fn-goal-structuring-notation]: **Goal Structuring Notation (GSN)**: @kelly2004goal presented a graphical notation for safety arguments that represents the claims being asserted, the strategies that decompose them, the operational context and assumptions under which they hold, and the empirical evidence that supports them. Structuring an argument explicitly uncovers claims lacking supporting evidence or unverified operational assumptions, which are the gaps that @tbl-vol3-safety-case is designed to expose. \index{Goal Structuring Notation!safety case}

A *claim* asserts a specific operational property, such as authorization validity or idempotency. An *argument* links the architecture and runtime mechanisms to that claim. *Evidence* supplies the backing, in the form of audit logs, telemetry windows, regression suites, and operator review traces. As assurance-case methodology emphasizes [@lipson2013assurance], citing a governance tool or testing practice is not enough; the case must show enforcement, coverage, and relevance to the artifact actually deployed, and it records assumptions and counterexamples so that reviewers can see where the argument stops.

### The incident safety case {#sec-vol3-conclusion-incident-safety-case}

Showing that `op_42` restored latency on `db_primary_01` during `health_window_42` does not prove that the remediation agent is safe to run on arbitrary database incidents. @Tbl-vol3-safety-case scopes the safety case for `incident_42` to the mediated database change and its observed outcome, combining runtime records with the validation suites a production case requires so that each row states what the case must verify rather than asserting that every offline test ran during the live incident.

| Scoped claim                                                                                             | Argument and owner                                                                                                                                            | Supporting evidence                                                                                                                                       | Assumptions and residual uncertainty                                                                                                                                                                  |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| The mediated change to `db_primary_01` requires approval for the exact request and current preconditions | The action gate checks `approval_42` against `change_request_42`, its target, desired settings, expected `config_v7`, and validity conditions before dispatch | The approval and admission records, together with tests of missing, expired, mismatched, and stale approvals                                              | The argument depends on controlled access paths and endpoint enforcement; an unrelated privileged operator or bypass is outside this particular gate's claim                                          |
| The lost response does not justify issuing a fresh duplicate change                                      | The settlement process preserves `op_42` for `operations_owner_42` and reconciles through the endpoint's operation-status and deduplication contract          | Durable intent and recovery descriptor recorded before dispatch; the lost-response status; the later source confirmation that `op_42` applied `config_v8` | The endpoint must honor the stated identity, atomic version check, and retention contract, including delayed requests; unavailable status leaves the operation unresolved rather than proving failure |
| The incident meets `incident_contract_v1` under the recorded acceptance scope                            | The acceptance owner checks the applied configuration, required change-policy conditions, and the declared service measurement window                         | `acceptance_42` references `op_42`, `config_v8`, `health_window_42`, required checks, and the authorized adopter                                          | Measurements cover the named service and window, not every future condition; they do not prove the model's diagnosis, and post-window monitoring remains with `operations_owner_42`                   |

: **An Incident Safety Case in Three Claims**: Mechanisms, records, and assumptions support different parts of the argument. Evidence sufficient for one claim does not automatically establish the others. {#tbl-vol3-safety-case}

An agent's diagnostic report can point engineers to anomalous telemetry or inconsistent logs, but it cannot prove its own successful execution. A recorded operator sign-off counts as evidence only where the contract requires it, and human review has its own failure modes and blind spots, so it needs the same provenance and scope checks as an automated assertion.

### Release evidence and staged exposure {#sec-vol3-conclusion-release-evidence}

The three claims of @tbl-vol3-safety-case concern one execution. Releasing the configuration that handled it is a population question, answered by the staged offline, shadow, and canary evidence of @sec-vol3-evaluation-releases under causal and statistical release evidence (principle \ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}). In that comparison `incident_42` counts as a single trial, and halving the detectable difference between two configurations quadruples the tasks per arm (@eq-vol3-eval-planning-power), so one incident cannot settle a release. Had `op_42` stayed unknown at the observation cutoff, that trial would count as unresolved even if latency later recovered, because healthy telemetry on one service does not settle an outstanding effect.

Staged exposure carries the limit the incident showed. Stopping a canary, revoking its tokens, or draining its traffic halts only future dispatches; a request the endpoint has already applied, as it applied `op_42` before the reply was lost, persists with its settlement owner. A release safety case therefore documents how partially executed work is contained and settled rather than assuming that rolling back a container image restores world state.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Tripwires that stop admission, and rollback that leaves transmitted requests and changed objects in place, are established in @sec-vol3-evaluation-releases-tripwires.
:::

### Evidence preservation under policy change {#sec-vol3-feedback-stability}

An incident trace does not automatically belong in a learning pipeline. If an engineer proposes extracting a segment as `training_record_42`, the training admission predicates decide whether its context, targets, permissions, and provenance qualify, and an unresolved or aborted trace is not a negative example; labeling it as one biases the learned policy. Validation suites must also stay out of the training loop, because repeatedly selecting policies against the same evaluation set erodes its statistical validity [@dwork2015reusable]. Here the verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) meets release evidence (principle \ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}). Once a verification metric becomes a training loss or reward, it loses its standing as an independent assessment. This is Goodhart's law in the form @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-pressure met it under search and @sec-vol3-rlvr-score-intended-outcome met it under training. Optimization concentrates on the verifier's blind spots, so release evidence must come from checks the optimization never observed.\index{Goodhart's law!verifier as reward}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The admission predicates for a training record, covering record fidelity, permitted use, process and outcome conditions, and target suitability, are established in @sec-vol3-verifier-funnel.
:::

Updating model weights or prompts produces a new configuration that needs fresh release evidence, not an endorsement inherited from past incidents. A weight update also invalidates serving state, since KV tensors computed under the old weights are not valid for the new model even when the prefix text is identical. The safety case therefore binds to the exact configuration scheduled for deployment, and the resolution of `incident_42` remains an audit of one execution, not a clearance for later versions.

::: {#chk-19-safety-cases-and-blast-radius .callout-checkpoint title="Defend the incident's acceptance"}

Each prompt tests whether a piece of evidence supports the claim it is attached to.

- [ ] **Claim scope**: Which records establish that the approved change applied, and why is acceptable latency alone insufficient?
- [ ] **Missing evidence**: If operation status remains unavailable, what must stay unresolved and who retains responsibility?
- [ ] **Evidence quality**: How can a model report or human review contribute without becoming independent proof of every claimed property?
- [ ] **Evidence volume**: A team can afford only twice as many release tasks per arm. By @eq-vol3-eval-planning-power, by what factor does the smallest difference it can detect shrink, and is that enough to rank two configurations that differ by a few points?
- [ ] **Changed configuration**: Why do stopping candidate admissions and preserving the same prompt establish neither reversal of earlier effects nor compatibility of old KV state with new weights?

:::

An inspectable safety case makes the acceptance decision transparent and lists its residual risks, including states outside the measurement window, shifting workloads, and unverified edge cases, as explicit design constraints. Naming these limits is not an admission of failure, because a case that names its limits is the only kind a reviewer can check.

## Open Questions Within the Digital Boundary {#sec-vol3-conclusion-frontiers}
